claim: Glutamine synthetases (GS) are central enzymes essential for the nitrogen metabolism across all domains of life.
source: Glutamine synthetases (GS) are central enzymes essential for the nitrogen metabolism across all domains of life.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the role of glutamine synthetases.

claim: In the methanogenic archaeon Methanosarcina mazei, the metabolite 2-oxoglutarate (2-OG) directly induces the GS activity.
source: In the methanogenic archaeon Methanosarcina mazei, it has been shown that the metabolite 2-oxoglutarate (2-OG) directly induces the GS activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and is further investigated in this manuscript.

claim: The strong activation of M. mazei GS (GlnA1) by 2-OG is based on the 2-OG dependent dodecamer assembly of GlnA1.
source: Here, we show that the strong activation of M. mazei GS (GlnA1) by 2-OG is based on the 2-OG dependent dodecamer assembly of GlnA1 by using mass photometry (MP) and single particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) analysis of purified strep-tagged GlnA1.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass photometry and cryo-EM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The dodecamer assembly from dimers occurred without any detectable intermediate oligomeric state.
source: The dodecamer assembly from dimers occurred without any detectable intermediate oligomeric state and was not affected in the presence of GlnK1.
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data showing direct transition from dimers to dodecamers.

claim: The dodecamer assembly was not affected in the presence of GlnK1.
source: The dodecamer assembly from dimers occurred without any detectable intermediate oligomeric state and was not affected in the presence of GlnK1.
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry experiments with and without GlnK1.

claim: The 2.39 Å cryo-EM structure of the dodecameric complex in the presence of 12.5 mM 2-OG demonstrated that 2-OG is binding between two monomers.
source: The 2.39 Å cryo-EM structure of the dodecameric complex in the presence of 12.5 mM 2-OG demonstrated that 2-OG is binding between two monomers.
evidence: This is directly supported by the cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: 2-OG appears to induce the dodecameric assembly in a cooperative way.
source: Thereby, 2-OG appears to induce the dodecameric assembly in a cooperative way.
evidence: This is inferred from the assembly kinetics and structural data.

claim: The active site is primed by an allosteric interaction cascade caused by 2-OG-binding towards an adaption of an open active state conformation.
source: Furthermore, the active site is primed by an allosteric interaction cascade caused by 2-OG-binding towards an adaption of an open active state conformation.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons between different conformational states.

claim: In the presence of additional glutamine, strong feedback inhibition of GS activity was observed.
source: In the presence of additional glutamine, strong feedback inhibition of GS activity was observed.
evidence: This is supported by activity assay data with glutamine supplementation.

claim: Glutamine dependent disassembly of the dodecamer was excluded by MP.
source: Since glutamine dependent disassembly of the dodecamer was excluded by MP, feedback inhibition most likely relies on the binding of glutamine to the catalytic site.
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data showing no change in oligomeric state with glutamine.

claim: Feedback inhibition most likely relies on the binding of glutamine to the catalytic site.
source: Since glutamine dependent disassembly of the dodecamer was excluded by MP, feedback inhibition most likely relies on the binding of glutamine to the catalytic site.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that glutamine does not cause disassembly but does inhibit activity.

claim: Under nitrogen limitation the induction of M. mazei GS into a catalytically active dodecamer is not affected by GlnK1 and crucially depends on the presence of 2-OG.
source: Based on our findings, we propose that under nitrogen limitation the induction of M. mazei GS into a catalytically active dodecamer is not affected by GlnK1 and crucially depends on the presence of 2-OG.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on 2-OG dependence and GlnK1 independence.

claim: Under nitrogen (N) sufficiency, glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) is active and generates glutamate from 2-OG and ammonium.
source: Under nitrogen (N) sufficiency, glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) is active and generates glutamate from 2-OG and ammonium (reviewed in van Heeswijk et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Under N limitation, low ammonium concentrations lead to an inactive GDH as a result of its low ammonium affinity.
source: Under N limitation however, low ammonium concentrations lead to an inactive GDH as a result of its low ammonium affinity, whereas the expression of GS is strongly induced in response to N limitation (Bolay et al., 2018; Gunka and Commichau, 2012; Stadtman, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The expression of GS is strongly induced in response to N limitation.
source: Under N limitation however, low ammonium concentrations lead to an inactive GDH as a result of its low ammonium affinity, whereas the expression of GS is strongly induced in response to N limitation (Bolay et al., 2018; Gunka and Commichau, 2012; Stadtman, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Under low ammonium conditions, GS together with glutamate synthase (GOGAT) are responsible for ammonium assimilation via the GS/GOGAT pathway.
source: Consequently, under low ammonium conditions, GS together with glutamate synthase (GOGAT) are responsible for ammonium assimilation via the GS/GOGAT pathway, one of the major intersections in central carbon and N metabolism.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nitrogen metabolism pathways.

claim: GS present across all domains of life plays a central role in cellular N assimilation under low N availability.
source: Accordingly, GS present across all domains of life plays a central role in cellular N assimilation under low N availability.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of GS.

claim: Most of the GS are grouped into three major classes based on their monomeric size and oligomerization properties.
source: Most of the GS are grouped into three major classes based on their monomeric size and oligomerization properties (overview in dos Santos Moreira et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.

claim: GSI and GSIII, both found in bacteria and archaea, mostly form dodecamers.
source: GSI and GSIII, both found in bacteria and archaea, mostly form dodecamers, whereas GSII found in Eukaryotes form decamers of smaller subunits (dos Santos Moreira et al., 2019; He et al., 2009; Valentine et al., 1968; van Rooyen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: GSII found in Eukaryotes form decamers of smaller subunits.
source: GSI and GSIII, both found in bacteria and archaea, mostly form dodecamers, whereas GSII found in Eukaryotes form decamers of smaller subunits (dos Santos Moreira et al., 2019; He et al., 2009; Valentine et al., 1968; van Rooyen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The GSI class can be further grouped into Iα-type GS and Iβ-type GS based on their amino acid sequence and respective molecular mechanisms of activity regulation.
source: The GSI class can be further grouped into Iα-type GS and Iβ-type GS based on their amino acid sequence and respective molecular mechanisms of activity regulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GS classification.

claim: Iß-type GS contain a conserved adenylylation site (Tyr397 residue near the active site), that allows for covalent modification of Iβ-type GS and leads to inactivation of the enzyme.
source: Iß-type GS contain a conserved adenylylation site (Tyr397 residue near the active site), that allows for covalent modification of Iβ-type GS and leads to inactivation of the enzyme (Brown et al., 1994; Magasanik, 1993; Shapiro and Stadtman, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Iα-type GS are not covalently modified and mainly show feedback inhibition by end products of the glutamine metabolism, including glutamine.
source: Iα-type GS on the other hand are not covalently modified and mainly show feedback inhibition by end products of the glutamine metabolism, including glutamine (Fisher, 1999; Gunka and Commichau, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: In gram-negative bacteria, mainly transcriptional activation of the coding gene (glnA) under low nitrogen availability occurs via a transcriptional activator (e.g. NtrC in Escherichia coli).
source: In gram-negative bacteria, mainly transcriptional activation of the coding gene (glnA) under low nitrogen availability occurs via a transcriptional activator (e.g. NtrC in Escherichia coli Jiang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: For several gram-positive bacteria, the mechanism of regulation is a de-repression of glnA transcription under N limitation, which has also been shown for methanoarchaea.
source: For several gram-positive bacteria however, the mechanism of regulation is a de-repression of glnA transcription under N limitation, which has also been shown for methanoarchaea (Cohen-Kupiec et al., 1999; Fedorova et al., 2013; Fisher, 1999; Fisher and Wray, 2008; Hauf et al., 2016; Weidenbach et al., 2010; Weidenbach et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Signal perception and transduction in methanoarchaea occurs directly via the small effector molecule 2-OG, which increases under N limitation.
source: Whereas in gram positives the signal perception is complex and often also involves protein interactions of GS with transcriptional regulators (reviewed in Gunka and Commichau, 2012), signal perception and transduction in methanoarchaea occurs directly via the small effector molecule 2-OG, which increases under N limitation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about methanoarchaeal nitrogen regulation.

claim: Binding of 2-OG to the global N repressor protein NrpR significantly changes the repressor conformation resulting in dissociation from its respective operator.
source: It has been shown that binding of 2-OG to the global N repressor protein NrpR significantly changes the repressor conformation resulting in dissociation from its respective operator (Lie et al., 2007; Weidenbach et al., 2010; Wisedchaisri et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The activity of GS is strictly regulated in all organisms in response to changing N availabilities.
source: In addition to expression regulation, the activity of GS is also strictly regulated in all organisms in response to changing N availabilities, however, the underlying molecular mechanism(s) of inhibition significantly differ for the various GS classes and in various organisms (Reitzer, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Yeast GS (ScGS) is regulated via feedback inhibition by glutamine and additionally is susceptible to proteolytic degradation under N starvation.
source: For example, yeast GS (ScGS) is regulated via feedback inhibition by glutamine and additionally is susceptible to proteolytic degradation under N starvation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast GS regulation.

claim: Yeast GS was found to assemble into nanotubes.
source: It was also found to assemble into nanotubes (He et al., 2009) and under advanced cellular starvation into inactive filaments (Petrovska et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: In E. coli, the activity of the Iß-type GS (EcGS) is controlled by cumulative feedback inhibition and covalent modification.
source: In E. coli, the activity of the Iß-type GS (EcGS) is controlled by cumulative feedback inhibition and covalent modification (reviewed in Reitzer, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.

claim: Each of the 12 subunits of E. coli GS can be modified by adenylylation (Tyr397) resulting in an inactivation of the respective subunit.
source: It has been shown that each of the 12 subunits can be modified by adenylylation (Tyr397) resulting in an inactivation of the respective subunit (Stadtman, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The adenlylylation of single subunits makes the other subunits more susceptible to cumulative feedback inhibition by various substances.
source: Moreover, the adenlylylation of single subunits makes the other subunits more susceptible to cumulative feedback inhibition by various substances (Stadtman, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The dodecameric structure of EcGS has been known for a long time.
source: The dodecameric structure of EcGS has been known for a long time (Almassy et al., 1986; Yamashita et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: When artificially exposed to divalent cations (Mn2+, Co2+), E. coli GS randomly aggregates and produces long hexagonal tubes (paracrystalline aggregates).
source: However, when artificially exposed to divalent cations (Mn2+, Co2+), it randomly aggregates and produces long hexagonal tubes (paracrystalline aggregates) (Valentine et al., 1968).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The B. subtilis GS has been shown to be feedback regulated.
source: The B. subtilis GS has been shown to be feedback regulated.
evidence: This is established knowledge about B. subtilis GS.

claim: Binding of the transcriptional repressor GlnR to the feedback inhibited B. subtilis GS complex not only activates the transcription repression function of GlnR but also stabilizes the inactive GS conformation potentially changing from a dodecamer into a tetradecameric structure.
source: In addition, binding of the transcriptional repressor GlnR to the feedback inhibited complex not only activates the transcription repression function of GlnR (Fisher and Wray, 2008), but also stabilizes the inactive GS conformation potentially changing from a dodecamer into a tetradecameric structure (Travis et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: M. mazei is a mesophilic methanoarchaeon which is able to fix N2.
source: In M. mazei, a mesophilic methanoarchaeon which is able to fix N2, regulation of the central N metabolism has been studied extensively on the transcriptional and post-transcriptional level (Jäger et al., 2009; Prasse and Schmitz, 2018; Veit et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about M. mazei.

claim: A central role of 2-OG for the perception of changes in N availabilities has been proposed for M. mazei, as has been demonstrated for cyanobacteria.
source: A central role of 2-OG for the perception of changes in N availabilities has been proposed, as has been demonstrated for cyanobacteria (Forchhammer, 1999; Herrero et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: M. mazei GlnA1 is not covalently modified in response to N availability and thus represents an Iα-type-GS.
source: GlnA1 is not covalently modified in response to N availability and thus represents an Iα-type-GS (Ehlers et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: GlnA1 is directly activated under N starvation by the high intracellular concentrations of the metabolite 2-OG.
source: It has been proposed, that GlnA1 is directly activated under N starvation by the high intracellular concentrations of the metabolite 2-OG (Ehlers et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: 2-OG represents the internal signal for N limitation, since the internal 2-OG level significantly increases due to missing consumption by GDH under N starvation.
source: 2-OG represents the internal signal for N limitation, since the internal 2-OG level significantly increases due to missing consumption by GDH under N starvation (M. mazei contains the oxidative TCA part, anabolic).
evidence: This is established knowledge about metabolic regulation in M. mazei.

claim: The increased cellular 2-OG concentration has been shown to be directly perceived by GlnA1, most likely by direct binding resulting in strong activation.
source: The increased cellular 2-OG concentration has been shown to be directly perceived by GlnA1, most likely by direct binding resulting in strong activation (Ehlers et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Two small proteins interact with M. mazei GlnA1, the PII-like protein GlnK1 and small protein sP26 comprising 23 amino acids.
source: Besides, we showed first evidence that two small proteins interact with M. mazei GlnA1, the PII-like protein GlnK1 and small protein sP26 comprising 23 amino acids (Ehlers et al., 2005; Gutt et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: In the absence of 2-OG, the GlnA1/GlnK1 complexes are more stable than in the presence of high 2-OG.
source: Moreover, initial complex formation analysis by a pull-down approach indicated that in the absence of 2-OG, the GlnA1/GlnK1 complexes are more stable than in the presence of high 2-OG.
evidence: This is based on previous experimental observations.

claim: Schumacher et al. propose a regulation of GlnA1 activity by oligomeric modulation, with GlnK1 stabilizing the dodecameric structure and the formation of GlnA1 active sites.
source: Based on their findings, Schumacher et al. propose a regulation of GlnA1 activity by oligomeric modulation, with GlnK1 stabilizing the dodecameric structure and the formation of GlnA1 active sites.
evidence: This is a claim from another study cited in the manuscript.

claim: Strep-tagged purified GlnA1 analyzed by size exclusion chromatography (SEC) in the presence of 12.5 mM 2-OG is exclusively present in a dodecameric structure.
source: The strep-tagged purified GlnA1 was analyzed by size exclusion chromatography (SEC) in the presence of 12.5 mM 2-OG, demonstrating that GS is exclusively present in a dodecameric structure, no other oligomers were detectable (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by SEC data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: In the presence of low 2-OG concentrations (0.1 mM) all of the M. mazei GlnA1 was nearly exclusively present as dimers with no higher molecular weight complexes present.
source: Strep-tagged purified GlnA1 (after SEC) was dialyzed into a 2-OG free HEPES buffer (see Materials and Methods) and subsequently analyzed by MP, demonstrating that in the presence of low 2-OG concentrations (0.1 mM) all of the M. mazei GlnA1 was nearly exclusively present as dimers with no higher molecular weight complexes present.
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data.

claim: After the addition of 12.5 mM 2-OG, the size distribution shifted towards a higher molecular weight complex of 630–700 kDa corresponding to a fully assembled dodecamer species.
source: After the addition of 12.5 mM 2-OG, the size distribution shifted towards a higher molecular weight complex of 630–700 kDa (calculated based on the measured dimer size in each measurement; expected molecular weight of dodecamer: 634 kDa) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The effective concentration of 2-OG for dodecamer assembly is EC50=0.75 ± 0.01 mM 2-OG.
source: This allowed to determine the effective concentration of 2-OG for dodecamer assembly to be EC50=0.75 ± 0.01 mM 2-OG (based on two biological replicates, calculated with the percentage of dodecamer) as described in Materials and Methods, and further verified that no other intermediate oligomeric complexes were detectable during dodecameric assembly (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is calculated from mass photometry titration data.

claim: No other intermediate oligomeric complexes were detectable during dodecameric assembly.
source: This allowed to determine the effective concentration of 2-OG for dodecamer assembly to be EC50=0.75 ± 0.01 mM 2-OG (based on two biological replicates, calculated with the percentage of dodecamer) as described in Materials and Methods, and further verified that no other intermediate oligomeric complexes were detectable during dodecameric assembly (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data.

claim: GlnA1 did not reach 100% dodecamer assembly after removal and re-addition of 2-OG, although only dodecameric GlnA1 was used for dialysis.
source: Notably, GlnA1 did not reach 100% dodecamer assembly after removal and re-addition of 2-OG, although only dodecameric GlnA1 was used for dialysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is an observation from mass photometry experiments.

claim: GlnA1 is rather unstable in the absence of 2-OG and some of the protein lost its ability to oligomerize after 2-OG was removed by dialysis.
source: We conclude that GlnA1 is rather unstable in the absence of 2-OG and some of the protein lost its ability to oligomerize after 2-OG was removed by dialysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that not all protein reassembles after 2-OG removal and re-addition.

claim: The specific activity of purified strep-tagged GlnA1 increased from 0.0 U/mg in the absence of 2-OG up to 7.8 ± 1.7 U/mg in the presence of 12.5 mM 2-OG.
source: Activity measurements of Strep-GlnA1 in the presence of increasing 2-OG concentrations showed a strong increase from 0.0 U/mg in the absence of 2-OG up to 7.8 ± 1.7 U/mg in the presence of 12.5 mM 2-OG (six independent protein purifications).
evidence: This is supported by activity assay data.

claim: The EC50 for GlnA1 activity was determined to be 6.3 mM 2-OG.
source: The EC50 for GlnA1 activity was determined to be 6.3 mM 2-OG (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is calculated from activity assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 2-OG first acts as a trigger for dodecameric assembly of M. mazei GlnA1 (with an EC50=0.75 mM 2-OG), setting it apart from other bacterial and eukaryotic enzyme variants.
source: Thus, we conclude that 2-OG first acts as a trigger for dodecameric assembly of M. mazei GlnA1 (with an EC50=0.75 mM 2-OG), setting it apart from other bacterial and eukaryotic enzyme variants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing assembly and activity EC50 values.

claim: In addition to the dodecameric assembly, 2-OG is required for a further 2-OG-induced conformational switch of the active site.
source: Moreover, most likely in addition to the dodecameric assembly, 2-OG is required for a further 2-OG-induced conformational switch of the active site, since saturated GlnA1 activities are not reached in the presence of 5 mM 2-OG, when most of the GlnA1 is in a dodecameric structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference between assembly and activity EC50 values.

claim: For full activity, the presence of at least 12.5 mM 2-OG is required (EC50=6.3 mM 2-OG).
source: For full activity, the presence of at least 12.5 mM 2-OG is required (EC50=6.3 mM 2-OG).
evidence: This is supported by activity assay data.

claim: In the absence of 2-OG varying ratios between GlnA1 and GlnK1 (20:1, 2:1, 2:10) did not result in any dodecamer assembly of GlnA1.
source: Performing the MP analysis under the tested conditions as before but in the presence of purified GlnK1, demonstrated that (i) in the absence of 2-OG varying ratios between GlnA1 and GlnK1 (20:1, 2:1, 2:10 calculated based on monomer mass) did not result in any dodecamer assembly of GlnA1 (Figure 2A and B)
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: No difference in the GlnA1 dodecameric assembly in the presence of 2-OG was obtained in the presence of purified GlnK1 (ratio 2:1).
source: (ii) no difference in the GlnA1 dodecameric assembly in the presence of 2-OG was obtained in the presence of purified GlnK1 (ratio 2:1)
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data.

claim: No binding of GlnK1 to GlnA1 was detected by a respective increase in the mass of the higher oligomeric complex.
source: (iii) nor was binding of GlnK1 to GlnA1 detected by a respective increase in the mass of the higher oligomeric complex (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data showing no mass increase upon GlnK1 addition.

claim: The presence of GlnK1 (ratio 2:1) had no influence on the 2-OG affinity (EC50 (- GlnK1)=1.06 mM 2-OG; EC50 (+ GlnK1)=1.02 mM 2-OG).
source: Moreover, the presence of GlnK1 (ratio 2:1) neither had an influence on the 2-OG affinity (EC50 (- GlnK1)=1.06 mM 2-OG; EC50 (+ GlnK1)=1.02 mM 2-OG, EC50 calculated based on the dodecamer/dimer ratio)
evidence: This is calculated from mass photometry titration data with and without GlnK1.

claim: GlnK1 had no effect in any ratio on the specific activity of GlnA1.
source: nor in any ratio on the specific activity of GlnA1 (Figure 2D and E: exemplarily showing 2:1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by activity assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Under the conditions tested using purified proteins, GlnA1 dodecamer assembly occurs independently of GlnK1 and no binding of GlnK1 to the dodecameric GlnA1 occurs.
source: Consequently, we conclude that under the conditions tested using purified proteins, GlnA1 dodecamer assembly occurs independently of GlnK1 and no binding of GlnK1 to the dodecameric GlnA1 occurs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mass photometry and activity assay data.

claim: Cellular components/metabolites not present in these experiments may be crucial for a GlnA1-GlnK1 interaction.
source: However, we cannot exclude that cellular components/metabolites not present in these experiments are crucial for a GlnA1-GlnK1 interaction.
evidence: This is speculation about potential missing factors in the in vitro experiments.

claim: A 2.39 Å resolution structure of GlnA1 was achieved revealing well-resolved side chains that facilitated seamless model building.
source: Leveraging this dataset, we aligned the particles to a 2.39 Å resolution structure, revealing well-resolved side chains that facilitated seamless model building (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: GlnA1 assembles into a dodecamer characterized by stacked hexamer rings.
source: The detailed structural analysis uncovered that GlnA1 assembles into a dodecamer characterized by stacked hexamer rings.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: A single GlnA1 protomer is composed of 15 β-strands and 15 α-helices and is split into a larger C-domain and an N-domain by helix α3.
source: A single GlnA1 protomer is composed of 15 β-strands and 15 α-helices and is split into a larger C-domain and an N-domain by helix α3.
evidence: This is determined from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The structures are highly similar to Gram-positive bacterial GS structures (PDB: 4lnn), with root mean squared deviations (rmsds) of 0.5–1.0 Å.
source: The structures are highly similar to Gram-positive bacterial GS structures (PDB: 4lnn, Murray et al., 2013), with root mean squared deviations (rmsds) of 0.5–1.0 Å.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with known structures.

claim: Density for the bound 2-OG is localized at an allosteric site at the interface between two GlnA1 protomers in vicinity of the GlnA1 catalytic site.
source: A closer inspection of the density reveals the density for the bound 2-OG at an allosteric site localized at the interface between two GlnA1 protomers in vicinity of the GlnA1 catalytic site (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM density map.

claim: R172' and S189' coordinate the γ-Carboxy-group of 2-OG.
source: R172' and S189' coordinate the γ-Carboxy-group.
evidence: This is determined from the cryo-EM structure showing 2-OG binding interactions.

claim: R26 is coordinating the α-Keto-group and, together with R87 and R173', the α-Carboxy group of 2-OG.
source: Latter arginine is coordinating the α-Keto-group and, together with R87 and R173', the α-Carboxy group of 2-OG (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is determined from the cryo-EM structure showing 2-OG binding interactions.

claim: F24 stabilizes the 2-OG via stacking with its phenyl ring.
source: Notably, F24 stabilizes the 2-OG via stacking with its phenyl ring (Figure 5).
evidence: This is determined from the cryo-EM structure showing 2-OG binding interactions.

claim: This binding contribution from two GlnA1 protomers at the intersubunit junction enhances activation by boosting readiness and the rate of full complex assembly.
source: This binding contribution from two GlnA1 protomers at the intersubunit junction enhances activation by boosting readiness and the rate of full complex assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation of 2-OG binding at the interface.

claim: 2-OG operates akin to molecular glue that facilitate the observed cooperative assembly.
source: It operates akin to molecular glue that facilitate the observed cooperative assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional data.

claim: The catalytically important residues in M. mazei are the aspartic acid (D57), that abstracts the proton from ammonium, and the catalytic glutamic acid, Glu307.
source: A comparison with the substrate-bound GlnA1 structure (PDB: 8tfk, Schumacher et al., 2023) revealed that the catalytically important residues in M. mazei are the aspartic acid (D57), that abstracts the proton from ammonium, and the catalytic glutamic acid, Glu307.
evidence: This is determined by comparison with a substrate-bound structure.

claim: The active site of M. mazei GlnA1 is formed at the interface between two subunits in the hexamer and formed by five key catalytic elements: the E flap, the Y loop, the N loop, the Y* loop and the D50'́ loop.
source: The active site of M. mazei GlnA1 is formed at the interface between two subunits in the hexamer and formed by five key catalytic elements surrounding the active site: the E flap (residues 303–310), the Y loop (residues 369–377), the N loop (residues 235–247), the Y* loop (residues 152–161) and the D50'́ loop (residues 56–71).
evidence: This is determined from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: 2-OG binding triggers movements that lead to structural changes in the substrate binding pocket.
source: Superposition of our structure with the apo-M. mazei structure (PDB: 8tfb, Schumacher et al., 2023) reveals that 2-OG binding also triggers further movements that lead to structural changes in the substrate binding pocket (Figure 5A, B and D).
evidence: This is determined by structural comparison between 2-OG-bound and apo structures.

claim: R87' and its loop undergo a dramatic flip to coordinate 2-OG and D170 of helix α3.
source: R87' and its loop undergo a dramatic flip to coordinate 2-OG and D170 of helix α3 (residues 167–181) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is observed by comparing 2-OG-bound and apo structures.

claim: Helix α3 shifts forward, causing F184 to flip over and facilitate a T-shaped aromatic interaction with F202.
source: Notably, helix α3 shifts forward, causing F184 to flip over and facilitate a T-shaped aromatic interaction with F202.
evidence: This is observed by comparing 2-OG-bound and apo structures.

claim: The pull on F202 causes F204 to flip, allowing π-stacking with the purine moiety of ATP.
source: The resulting pull on F202 causes F204 to flip, allowing π-stacking with the purine moiety of ATP (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is observed by comparing structures and inferring ATP binding mode.

claim: This series of structural changes primes the active site for ATP binding by already adopting the side chain conformations that are observed in analog (Met-Sox-P-ADP)-bound structure (transition state).
source: This series of structural changes primes the active site for ATP binding by already adopting the side chain conformations that are observed in analog (Met-Sox-P-ADP)-bound structure (transition state) (PDB: 8tfk, Schumacher et al., 2023), thus facilitating nucleotide binding (Figure 5C and E).
evidence: This is determined by structural comparison with transition state structure.

claim: The D50' loop adopts a position similar to the transition state in a catalytic competent conformation.
source: Additionally, the D50' loop adopts a position similar to the transition state in a catalytic competent conformation.
evidence: This is determined by structural comparison.

claim: Compared to the apo structure, R66 flips out of the catalytic pocket, now accommodating R319 which participates in phosphoryl transfer catalysis.
source: Compared to the apo structure (Schumacher et al., 2023), R66 flips out of the catalytic pocket, now accommodating R319 which participates in phosphoryl transfer catalysis (Liaw and Eisenberg, 1994; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is determined by structural comparison and supported by citation.

claim: Asp 57' moves deeper into the binding site, facilitating the proton abstraction of NH4+ and preparing for its attack on the phosphorylated glutamate.
source: In addition, Asp 57' moves deeper into the binding site, facilitating the proton abstraction of NH4+ and preparing for its attack on the phosphorylated glutamate.
evidence: This is determined by structural comparison and inference about catalytic mechanism.

claim: The first feedback inhibition of an archaeal GS by glutamine has been reported for Methermicoccus shengliensis GS.
source: Very recently, the first feedback inhibition of an archaeal GS by glutamine has been reported for Methermicoccus shengliensis GS (Müller et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The specific arginine residue identified to be relevant for the feedback inhibition is R66.
source: The specific arginine residue identified to be relevant for the feedback inhibition is R66.
evidence: This is based on findings from another study.

claim: In the presence of 12.5 mM 2-OG, the R66A mutant protein showed the same specific activity as obtained for the wt.
source: In the presence of 12.5 mM 2-OG, the mutant protein showed the same specific activity as obtained for the wt.
evidence: This is supported by activity assay data comparing wildtype and mutant.

claim: When supplementing 5 mM glutamine, exclusively the wt was strongly feedback inhibited, whereas the R66A mutant protein was not significantly affected.
source: However, when supplementing 5 mM glutamine, exclusively the wt was strongly feedback inhibited, whereas the R66A mutant protein was not significantly affected (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by activity assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In B. subtilis, R62 is responsible for feedback inhibition.
source: In B. subtilis, R62 is responsible for feedback inhibition.
evidence: This is established knowledge about B. subtilis GS.

claim: The superposition of the apo-BsGS structure with the 2-OG-bound GlnA1 reveals a similar positioning of the respective M. mazei R66 indicating a similar mechanism.
source: The superposition of the apo-BsGS structure (PDB: 4lnn, Murray et al., 2013) with our 2-OG-bound GlnA1 reveals a similar positioning of the respective M. mazei R66 (Figure 6B) indicating a similar mechanism.
evidence: This is determined by structural comparison.

claim: Glutamine does not induce disassembly of the dodecameric wt GlnA1.
source: Moreover, we can rule out an effect on the oligomeric structure of GlnA1 by MP analysis, clearly showing that glutamine does not induce disassembly of the dodecameric wt GlnA1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: R66 is an important residue to bind to glutamine in the product state of the enzyme.
source: Instead, this effect can be explained with the role of R66 being an important residue to bind to glutamine in the product state of the enzyme.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutant data and structural information.

claim: In M. mazei, increased 2-OG concentrations act as a central N starvation signal.
source: In M. mazei, increased 2-OG concentrations act as a central N starvation signal (Ehlers et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Dimeric GlnA1 (apo GlnA1) is inactive and crucially requires 2-OG to form an active dodecameric complex.
source: We have found mainly dimeric GlnA1 (apo GlnA1) to be inactive and crucially require 2-OG to form an active dodecameric complex.
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry and activity assay data.

claim: The dodecameric conformation is the only active state of GlnA1.
source: Moreover, this dodecameric conformation is the only active state of GlnA1.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between dodecamer formation and activity.

claim: 2-OG assembles the dodecamer by binding at the interface of two subunits and functions as a molecular glue between neighboring subunits.
source: In the first step, 2-OG assembles the dodecamer by binding at the interface of two subunits (Figure 4B) and functions as a molecular glue between neighboring subunits.
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing 2-OG at the interface.

claim: The assembly upon 2-OG addition observed using MP appears to be cooperative, fast, and without any detectable intermediate states.
source: The assembly upon 2-OG addition observed using MP appears to be cooperative, fast, and without any detectable intermediate states (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data.

claim: Octameric complexes are most likely broken or disassembled GlnA1-dodecamers or dead-ends in assembly with no physiological function, rather than an incomplete dodecamer during assembly.
source: Consequently, octamers are most likely broken or disassembled GlnA1-dodecamers or dead-ends in assembly with no physiological function, rather than an incomplete dodecamer during assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that octamers are only seen in certain sample conditions and not in cryo-EM or SEC.

claim: The findings are contrary to the assembly model proposed by Schumacher et al., 2023.
source: Thus, our findings are contrary to the assembly model proposed by Schumacher et al., 2023.
evidence: This is a comparison with another published model.

claim: The allosteric binding of 2-OG causes a series of conformational changes in GlnA1 protomers, which prime the active site for the transition state and hence catalysis of the enzyme.
source: As a second step of activation, the allosteric binding of 2-OG causes a series of conformational changes in GlnA1 protomers, which prime the active site for the transition state and hence catalysis of the enzyme.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons showing conformational changes.

claim: The conformational change of the ATP-binding pocket of the dodecameric GlnA1 upon 2-OG binding goes hand in hand with the observed increased activity at higher 2-OG concentrations.
source: This conformational change of the ATP-binding pocket of the dodecameric GlnA1 upon 2-OG binding goes hand in hand with the observed increased activity at higher 2-OG concentrations (Figure 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between structural changes and activity data.

claim: 2-OG transfers GlnA1 into its open active state conformation.
source: Comparing our 2-OG-bound GlnA1 dodecameric structure and the dodecameric M. mazei GlnA1 transition state (PDB: 8tfk) and apo structures (PDB: 8ftb) reported by Schumacher et al., 2023, clearly demonstrates that 2-OG transfers GlnA1 into its open active state conformation (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: The conformation of the 2-OG-bound dodecamer resembled the transition state conformation (ADP-Met-Sox-bound complex) reported by Schumacher et al., even though in this case no ATP was added.
source: The conformation of our 2-OG-bound dodecamer resembled the transition state conformation (ADP-Met-Sox-bound complex) reported by Schumacher et al., even though in our case no ATP was added (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: Binding of 2-OG in one protomer-protomer interface of a dodecameric GS causes a cooperative domino effect in the hexameric ring of M. thermolithotrophicus GS.
source: In this report, which does not delineate dodecamer assembly at all, it was demonstrated that binding of 2-OG in one protomer-protomer interface of a dodecameric GS causes a cooperative domino effect in the hexameric ring of M. thermolithotrophicus GS (Müller et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a claim from another study cited in the manuscript.

claim: A 2-OG bound protomer undergoes a conformational change and thereby induces the same shift in its neighboring protomer.
source: A 2-OG bound protomer undergoes a conformational change and thereby induces the same shift in its neighboring protomer (Müller et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a claim from another study cited in the manuscript.

claim: M. mazei GlnA1 reaches maximal activity only at much higher 2-OG concentrations (EC50=6.3 mM 2-OG) and likely requires a fully 2-OG-occupied dodecamer for maximal activity.
source: On the other hand, M. mazei GlnA1 reaches maximal activity only at much higher 2-OG concentrations (EC50=6.3 mM 2-OG) and likely requires a fully 2-OG-occupied dodecamer for maximal activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the activity data showing higher EC50 for activity than assembly.

claim: The difference between the two EC50 values strongly points towards the dodecamer assembly being induced by only one 2-OG per hexameric ring, whilst the maximum activity requires one 2-OG in every 2-OG binding site.
source: The difference between the two EC50 values strongly points towards the dodecamer assembly being induced by only one 2-OG per hexameric ring, whilst the maximum activity requires one 2-OG in every 2-OG binding site (in agreement with roughly sixfold higher EC50).
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in EC50 values for assembly and activity.

claim: The high activities obtained by 2-OG saturation (up to 9 U/mg), in comparison with previously described M. mazei GlnA1 activities in the absence of 2-OG in a significantly lower range (mU/mg), support the conclusion that 2-OG is substantial for the GlnA1 active state.
source: The here obtained high activities by 2-OG saturation (up to 9 U/mg), in comparison with previously described M. mazei GlnA1 activities in the absence of 2-OG in a significantly lower range (mU/mg) (Gutt et al., 2021; Schumacher et al., 2023), support our conclusion that 2-OG is substantial for the GlnA1 active state.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of activity data with previous studies.

claim: M. mazei GlnA1 belongs to the group of Iα-type GS, which are known to be feedback inhibited.
source: M. mazei GlnA1 belongs to the group of Iα-type GS, which are known to be feedback inhibited.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GS classification.

claim: R66 is the key residue for feedback inhibition in M. mazei GlnA1.
source: We confirmed a strong feedback inhibition by a genetic approach and validated R66 to be the key residue for this inhibition (Figure 6) as suggested in Müller et al., 2024.
evidence: This is supported by mutant analysis data.

claim: The mechanism of feedback inhibition has been described in detail for B. subtilis GS where R62 plays the central role by binding glutamine and inducing a well-ordered inactive structure at the substrate-binding pocket upon glutamine-binding.
source: The mechanism of feedback inhibition has been described in detail for B. subtilis GS (Murray et al., 2013). There, R62 plays the central role by binding glutamine and inducing a well-ordered inactive structure at the substrate-binding pocket upon glutamine-binding (Murray et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The homologous M. mazei R66 likely conveys a similar way of inhibition to B. subtilis GS.
source: The homologous M. mazei R66 likely conveys a similar way of inhibition to B. subtilis GS (Figure 6B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from structural similarity and mutant data.

claim: GlnK1 was shown to interact with GlnA1 in vivo after a nitrogen upshift by pull-down approaches, pointing towards an inhibitory function of GlnK1 under shifting conditions from N limitation to N sufficiency.
source: Moreover, in previous reports, GlnK1 was shown to interact with GlnA1 in vivo after a nitrogen upshift by pull-down approaches (Ehlers et al., 2005), pointing towards an inhibitory function of GlnK1 under shifting conditions from N limitation to N sufficiency.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Neither an interaction with GlnK1, nor GlnK1 effects on GlnA1 complex formation analyzed by MP, nor an effect of GlnK1 on GlnA1 activity was detectable under the conditions used.
source: However, in the present study, neither an interaction with GlnK1, nor GlnK1 effects on GlnA1 complex formation analyzed by MP, nor an effect of GlnK1 on GlnA1 activity was detectable under the conditions used at varying 2-OG concentrations (0.1–12.5 mM) and ratios of GlnK1 to GlnA1 (20:1, 2:1, 2:10) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry and activity assay data.

claim: Yet unknown cellular factor(s) might be required for an interaction of GlnA1 with both small proteins, GlnK1 and sP26, which is difficult to simulate under in vitro conditions with purified proteins.
source: Because these attempts were unsuccessful, we speculate that yet unknown cellular factor(s) might be required for an interaction of GlnA1 with both small proteins, GlnK1 and sP26, which however is difficult to simulate under in vitro conditions with purified proteins.
evidence: This is speculation about why interactions were not observed in vitro.

claim: GlnA1 and GOGAT may experience metabolic coupling by sP26 and/or GlnK1, e.g., by being involved in recruiting or separating GOGAT from GlnA1.
source: Taking this into account, we speculate about a potential function of the two small proteins beyond GlnA1 inactivation or activation. Since the GlnA1 reaction is coupled to the GOGAT reaction (GS/GOGAT system) and the products of the two reactions replenish the substrates for one other, it is tempting to speculate that GlnA1 and GOGAT experience metabolic coupling by sP26 and/or GlnK1, e.g., by being involved in recruiting or separating GOGAT from GlnA1.
evidence: This is speculation about potential alternative functions of the small proteins.

claim: Filament-like structures of M. mazei GlnA1 were observed in cryo-EM and their structure was resolved at a resolution of 6.9 Å.
source: Interestingly, dependent on the ice thickness and on higher concentrated areas of the grids, we could also observe filament-like structures of M. mazei GlnA1 in cryo-EM and resolved their structure at a resolution of 6.9 Å (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data.

claim: GlnA1 filaments are also detectable in the cryo-EM images of Schumacher et al., 2023, but were not reported.
source: Such GlnA1 filaments are also detectable in the cryo-EM images of Schumacher et al., 2023, but were not reported.
evidence: This is an observation from another study's data.

claim: The filament interface is much alike the previously reported E. coli GS filament structures.
source: The filament interface is much alike the previously reported E. coli GS filament structures (Huang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with known filament structures.

claim: The physiological relevance of filamentation in M. mazei remains unresolved.
source: The physiological relevance of filamentation in M. mazei however remains unresolved and raises the question, whether an additional rapid modulation of GlnA1 activity through higher oligomeric states exists.
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty about the biological significance of the observed filaments.

claim: In yeast, GS filamentation was described as mostly depending on stress conditions.
source: In yeast for example, GS filamentation was described as mostly depending on stress conditions (Petrovska et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: 2-OG is the central activator of GlnA1 in M. mazei, which assembles the active dodecamer and induces a conformational switch towards an active open state.
source: Overall, we have confirmed 2-OG to be the central activator of GlnA1 in M. mazei, which assembles the active dodecamer and induces a conformational switch towards an active open state.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from all the experimental data.

claim: The 2-OG-triggered dodecameric assembly is novel and described exclusively for M. mazei GlnA1.
source: Though 2-OG has previously been reported as an on-switch for (methano)archaeal GS activity (Ehlers et al., 2005; Müller et al., 2024; Pedro-Roig et al., 2013), the 2-OG-triggered dodecameric assembly is novel and described exclusively for M. mazei GlnA1.
evidence: This is a conclusion comparing the findings with previous literature.

claim: Neither in cyanobacteria, enterobacteria or Bacillus has 2-OG been reported as the sole direct activator of the enzyme, nor is complex (dis-)assembly a mode of regulating GS activity in any other of these model organisms.
source: Neither in cyanobacteria, enterobacteria or Bacillus has 2-OG been reported as the sole direct activator of the enzyme, nor is complex (dis-)assembly a mode of regulating GS activity in any other of these model organisms.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of GS regulation in other organisms.

claim: The cyanobacterial, enterobacterial, and gram-positive GS are assumed to be present in the cell as active dodecamers.
source: The cyanobacterial, enterobacterial, and gram-positive GS are assumed to be present in the cell as active dodecamers (Almassy et al., 1986; Bolay et al., 2018; Deuel et al., 1970).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The GS regulation in M. mazei by a 2-OG triggered assembly is unique across all prokaryotic GS studied so far.
source: Consequently, the GS regulation in M. mazei by a 2-OG triggered assembly is unique across all prokaryotic GS studied so far.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison with known GS regulation mechanisms.

claim: The direct 2-OG activation and glutamine feedback inhibition of M. mazei GS are two fast, reversible, and very direct ways of reacting towards the changing N status of the cell.
source: The direct 2-OG activation and glutamine feedback inhibition of M. mazei GS are two fast, reversible, and very direct ways of reacting towards the changing N status of the cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing rapid assembly/disassembly and feedback inhibition.

claim: The direct activation through 2-OG without any required additional protein is a more simple and direct regulation of GS compared to other organisms.
source: We propose that the direct activation through 2-OG without any required additional protein, as it is the case for all other regulations, is a more simple and direct regulation of GS.
evidence: This is a proposal based on comparison with other regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Due to the evolutionary placement of methanoarchaea and haloarchaea, where a direct 2-OG regulation has been found exclusively, this may represent an ancient regulation.
source: Due to the evolutionary placement of methanoarchaea and haloarchaea, where a direct 2-OG regulation has been found exclusively, this may represent an ancient regulation.
evidence: This is speculation based on evolutionary considerations.
